first.rationale: Two of the three acute symptoms are onboarding completion (-4%) and activation (-6%), which are internal funnel problems the competitor's pricing does not directly explain. The onboarding-shortening belief (memory_86) is the one I intend to act on and it is recorded only in proximal terms — completion rate, time-to-value, early adoption — with no evidence that the lift survived into retained, qualified revenue. Under the triage invariant that makes it both maximally consequential and insufficiently supported for a long-term-revenue objective, so it is my first pull. My second pull is memory_73 (promotional pricing) because it is the obvious reflex response to the competitor and is the highest-risk belief in the set: it is credited with acquisition and revenue lift with no stated retention, margin, or cohort-quality follow-up, so it could be an unsustainable-revenue trap that would misdirect this single slot. I deliberately do not spend budget on memory_57 (already carries an explicit no-retention-harm check) or memory_44 (already framed in pipeline-quality terms, and enterprise sales assist does not address the SMB-side declines). memory_31 corroborates the signup-friction direction from a different angle, which is part of why the onboarding direction is my prior, but it is older and narrower and does not by itself close the downstream-value gap. Key risk I am explicitly carrying: shortening or stripping onboarding can inflate completion and activation while producing worse-configured, lower-intent accounts that churn later — a proximal-metric win that is a long-term-revenue loss. So I will run this as a standard powered experiment but instrument it with downstream guardrails (30/60-day retention, expansion, and qualified-revenue-per-cohort), and I will not treat a completion-rate lift alone as success. If the archive shows memory_86's original record measured only completion and never tracked cohorts to revenue, I will de-scope to a small guarded test rather than a broad rollout; if it shows memory_73 had durable retained revenue behind it, I will reconsider promotional pricing as the counter to the competitor.

mid.rationale: The archive resolved both pulls decisively and in opposite directions. exp_86 closes the downstream-value gap I flagged: the onboarding lift was not merely proximal — completion +13% and time-to-value -2.1 days were accompanied by 30-day retention +3%, so the cohort improved rather than merely enlarged. That is exactly the evidence I said I needed to run this at standard scale rather than de-scoping to a guarded test. exp_73 confirms the trap I suspected and is stronger than I feared: signup +31% and qualified revenue +18% sit on top of 30-day retention -12%, with the original record explicitly instructing that targeted discounting NOT be generalized as sustainable growth. Under a primary objective of sustainable long-term qualified revenue, promotional pricing is disqualified — it would have bought a quarter of headline numbers and a churned cohort at the first renewal, and the compressed memory_73 summary had stripped precisely the fact that reverses the decision. I am therefore matching the intervention to the diagnosis rather than to the competitor: two of the three symptoms (onboarding completion -4%, activation -6%) are internal funnel decay, and shortened onboarding is the one direction with verified retention-positive effect on that funnel. It is also upstream of activation, so a completion lift should propagate to the activation decline; memory_91 and memory_31 point the same way but remain unverified, so I treat them as directional support only, not as load-bearing. Residual uncertainty I am carrying: exp_86 was run in a pre-competitor market, and the -4% decline may be partly composition — price-shopping traffic that abandons onboarding regardless of length — in which case the lift will underperform its historical size. Retention was measured at 30 days, which is short of a renewal cycle, so the +3% is encouraging but not proof of durable value. I will run a standard powered experiment holding out a control, instrumenting completion, activation, and 30/60-day retention plus qualified-revenue-per-cohort, and I will not ship on completion rate alone. I explicitly leave the competitor's SMB pricing pressure unanswered this cycle: the verified-correct response to it is not a discount, and losing some price-sensitive accounts is preferable to importing a cohort that churns. Enterprise sales assist (memory_44) stays queued as the unverified candidate most worth the next cycle's budget, since it addresses qualified-revenue mix without a discount.

final2.rationale: The competitor's second cut raises the urgency but changes none of the evidence, and I should not let escalation manufacture a conclusion the archive already ruled out. exp_73 is the single best-verified record I hold: a 40% targeted SMB discount bought signup +31% and qualified revenue +18% while taking 30-day retention -12%, with an explicit instruction not to generalize discounting as sustainable growth. A deeper competitor cut makes that worse, not better — matching price against an opponent who has just demonstrated willingness to go deeper invites a second round I lose, and it converts my remaining healthy SMB base onto discounted terms while importing a cohort that does not survive first renewal. Against a primary objective of sustainable long-term qualified revenue, that is spending the franchise to flatter one quarter. I therefore hold simplify_onboarding, which is the only direction with retention-positive verification (completion +13%, time-to-value -2.1 days, 30-day retention +3%), and which addresses the two symptoms that are actually mine rather than the competitor's: onboarding completion -4% and activation -6%. It is upstream of activation, so the lift should propagate. I want to be honest about what this decision does not do. It does not answer the churn conversations doubling this week. Onboarding improvements reach new and in-flight accounts, not existing price-sensitive customers already in a save conversation, so the acute retention bleed will continue through this cycle and leadership should hear that plainly rather than believe this experiment is a counter-offer. I also note a real distinction I cannot resolve without the archive: exp_73 tested an acquisition discount, whereas the present problem is retention of existing accounts, and a targeted save/concession motion is a different mechanism that might not carry the same -12% signature. That is a genuine gap, not a reason to act — I have zero evidence for retention discounting and the one adjacent record I hold argues against price as a durable lever, so the honest move is to queue it for verification next week rather than run it blind at the moment of maximum pressure. memory_57 (referral incentive, reportedly no retention harm in established customers) is the other unverified candidate that speaks to the existing base and belongs in that queue alongside memory_44. Further caveats I carry forward: exp_86 predates this competitive environment, its retention read is 30 days rather than a full renewal cycle, and part of the -4% may be composition from price-shopping traffic that abandons regardless of flow length, so I expect the historical effect size to be attenuated. I will hold out a control, instrument completion, activation, and 30/60-day retention plus qualified-revenue-per-cohort, and refuse to ship on completion rate alone. Accepting some loss of price-sensitive accounts is the deliberate cost of not buying revenue that churns.
